1.text: was spent, however, in war, and very little is known about the trade relations

2.text: of that period. I heard in the Anadyr that the bartering of iron arms to the

3.text: Chukchee was strictly forbidden, but that they bought kettles and cut iron

4.text: into knives and arrow-points. Even now old kettles are utilized in this manner.

5.text: Firelocks taken in battle were hammered with stones into rough spears.¹ At
5.note: Footnote 1 reference. mz/ocr (CATMuS) read the raised numeral as a plain '!'; the raster shows an ordinary raised '1', keyed as superscript U+00B9 per keying_spec.md §2.10 ("Key the actual Unicode superscript ... never the plain ASCII digit").

6.text: the present time the Chukchee make knives and adzes out of American files

7.text: by hammering them into the desired shape.

8.text: ANUI FAIR. — In 1788, forty-one years after the defeat of Pavlutsky, and
8.note: Run-in heading set in small capitals (full-height 'A'/'F', shorter following capitals); keyed as plain ASCII capitals per keying_spec.md §2.13 (second-level heading).

9.text: twenty-four years after the recall of the garrison from the fort of Anadyrsk,

10.text: Banner, the chief officer of the town of Sashiversk, on the Indighirka River,

11.text: who also held command over the Kolyma country, succeeded in establishing

12.text: anew peaceful relations with the western Reindeer Chukchee. As a result,
12.note: Zoomed (12@70) on a speck near 'Chukchee' that looked like a stray mark under 'k' in the composite thumbnail; at 2x it is an ordinary ink speck between letters, not a diacritic. No mark keyed.

13.text: a regular trade was started the following year. A few Chukchee were induced,

14.text: by means of gifts and promises, to subject themselves to Russian authority

15.text: and to pay tribute. The Chukchee were more anxious for trade than the

16.text: Russians. From the Anadyr came complaints that the people of the district

17.text: were forgotten by the Russians and did not get any wares. A tradition of

18.text: the Anui Chukchee relates that three Chukchee warriors took captive the

19.text: deputy of the Czarina,² and consented to release him only upon his promise
19.note: Footnote 2 reference. mz/ocr read the raised numeral as '?'; raster confirms an ordinary raised '2' (zoomed 19@30), keyed as superscript U+00B2 per keying_spec.md §2.10.

20.text: to establish an annual fair. After this, to appease his anger, they gave him

21.text: rich presents of black and blue fox-skins. The Chukchee fair was held at

22.text: irregular intervals, sometimes on the Dry Anui, near Mount Obrom, and at

23.text: a place called Ostrovnoye (“Insular”), sometimes on the Large Anui, near the

24.text: mouth of its affluent, the Angarka. Finally Ostrovnoye prevailed, because
24.note: mz/ocr rendered this as 'beçause' (cedilla-c); zoomed (24@85) and the raster shows an ordinary 'because', no mark under the c. Keyed as printed English, no diacritic.

25.text: the Chukchee were more numerous on the Dry Anui; moreover, travelling

26.text: on the Large Anui was difficult for dogs and reindeer because of the heavy

27.text: snowfalls; while the Dry Anui, which is contiguous to the tundra, is more

28.text: open to the winds. The Russians built at Ostrovnoye, a wooden fort called

29.text: Fort Anuisk. The fair grew rapidly in importance, and in the second decade

30.text: of the last century its traffic amounted to two hundred thousand rubles³ yearly,
30.note: Footnote 3 reference, superscript U+00B3, confirmed at 30@70 — raster shows an ordinary raised '3'.

31.text: which is a considerable sum in view of the scarcity of money in that period.

32.text: Some of the best peltries (such as beaver, marten, and lynx), muskrat and
32.note: mz/ocr read 'Iynx' (capital I); raster clearly shows lowercase 'lynx'.

33.text: marten garments, also a large portion of every kind of fox and polar-bear

34.text: skins and of walrus-tusks, came from the American shore. For instance, in

35.text: 1837, according to data contained in the official records found among the

36.text: archives of Kolyma, there were sold at the fair 100 beavers, 395 martens,

37.text: 30 lynxes, 31 marten garments, 13 musk-rat garments, etc., all from America,

38.text: since these animals are not found in Asia. To this must be added about

39.text: one-half of the 580 red foxes, 80 gray foxes, 13 black foxes, 268 white foxes,

40.text: 8 blue foxes, and 1563 walrus-tusks sold that year at the fair. These figures,

43.text: ³ A ruble is equivalent to about fifty cents.
